_doc: Editorial intros: 1-2 unique sentences framing each entry. Rendered above the verbatim Shackleton passage on the entry detail page. The intros are unique platform content (vs. the verbatim public-domain body) and de-duplicate the page for SEO purposes. Voice: neutral, factual, contextualizing — set the scene for the passage that follows.

intros.Into the Weddell Sea: Six weeks out from South Georgia, Endurance pushed south into the Weddell Sea pack — the same ice field that had stopped every previous attempt to reach the Antarctic continent from the east. Shackleton's December 7 entry records the first heavy ice the ship encountered, and the start of a six-week struggle through the floes that would end with the ship beset for good.
intros.The Ship in the Ice: By mid-January, Endurance had been working through the pack for over a month, gaining and losing ground with the drift. On January 19, 1915, at a position of 76°35′ South, the ice closed for the last time and the ship became immovable — the start of a ten-month drift toward open water that would never come.
intros.Endurance Crushed: Twenty-eight months after leaving England and ten months after first being beset, Endurance gave way to the pressure of the Weddell pack. The October 27 entry is the moment the expedition's plan ended and the survival journey began — five months on a drifting floe, an open-boat crossing of the Drake Passage, and a mountain traverse that nobody had ever attempted.
intros.Ocean Camp on the Ice: Six days after Endurance was abandoned, the party established Ocean Camp on a heavy floe about a mile from the wreck. Hurley's photographs of the camp survive only because he dove into the flooded ship to salvage the negatives; the floe itself drifted nearly six hundred nautical miles north before it began to break up the following spring.
intros.The James Caird Sets Out: From Elephant Island the nearest help lay eight hundred miles across the Drake Passage at the South Georgia whaling stations. On April 24, 1916, Shackleton, Worsley, Crean, McNeish, McCarthy, and Vincent set out in a 22-foot lifeboat reinforced with sledge runners and canvas — leaving twenty-two men on the beach with no certainty anyone would return.
intros.South Georgia at Last: The James Caird made South Georgia after seventeen days at sea — but landed on the uninhabited western coast, separated from the whaling stations by an unmapped mountain interior. The May 10 landfall in King Haakon Bay was a triumph that came with one more journey still to make.
intros.Crossing South Georgia: Shackleton, Worsley, and Crean left Peggotty Camp on the morning of May 19, 1916, and reached the Stromness whaling station thirty-six hours later — the first crossing of South Georgia's interior, made without sleep, without a proper map, and with brass screws driven through their boot soles for grip on the ice.
